utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Josse, are you ready to continue the examination of the witness Dicvic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. At some point, I know the registrar would like to deal with the Vasic exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When it is convenient for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I just asked the registrar to give me a copy of the provisional list he made. I'll first read through it and then we'll deal with it in open court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm ready to continue with my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Divcic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Divcic. I would like to remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. You'll now be further examined by Mr. Josse. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Divcic, we had got to the point in your evidence where you were beginning to tell the Chamber of the arrival in Pale of the Bosnian Serb leadership. You dealt in outline with conversations that you had with Mr. Karadzic. You've also mentioned that it was very cold, partly because of the altitude of Pale. Was Pale ready to become an administrative centre at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Pale was not ready for that. Pale is a tourist resort, some 10.000 or 12.000 people. They are some 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo. It's a rural area in the mountains. So the answer is absolutely no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did the leadership arrive in one go or did they arrive in dribs and drabs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In a very disorganised way, in dribs and drabs, and not only the leadership, but also many other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When people arrived, how were they accommodated, housed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In various ways. The local population -- because it was a difficult situation for everyone, well, they accepted to have in their places either friends or family, or sometimes unknown people. Many people lived in very inappropriate conditions then. But the most important thing was to have shelter, not to be in the open air.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you became involved in this logistical work in particular; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Firstly, why?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that it was a duty to help people who are in difficulty. That was the first reason. And then the second one was that I was the vice chair of the Serbian charity Dobrotvor, and immediately before we received, from Germany, a large donation through the German Red Cross. And part of that donation was given to Dobrotvor, part of it to Merhamet, and part to the Caritas, and a part of it, I think, to La Benevolencija. A gentleman by the name of Michael Steiner, who later on became the German representative in the contact group, well, he gave it to me, and the part that was given to Serbs, I decided to put it in various places, because even at that stage we did not have a warehouse for Dobrotvor. So part of it was in Pale and part of it in Vojkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll come back to this shipment or large amount of charity that had come from the Red Cross in a few moments' time, if I may. What I'd like to concentrate on first of all is whether you played any role in placing Bosnian Serb leaders in hotels, houses, and/or sorting out where administration was going to take place. That's where my question was directed and that's what I'd like you to turn your attention to first of all.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So could you tell the Chamber what you did in terms of sorting out accommodation for the leadership.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nearby, in Pale itself, that is, about a kilometre or two away, towards -- on the road towards Jahorina, there was a hotel that was built in 1984 for the Olympic Games. It had been closed, except for the winter season, and then a company from Kikinda was using it. And I knew that there in the neighbourhood lived local people who took care of that motel. I went to see them and I asked for the key, and they gave me the key, and I tried and organised the work of the Dobrotvor charity. And as people were coming in, I saw that they were disorganised. They had no place to stay. And then I started organising it with people whom I knew from different institutions, if that is your question. And there were other people who came, people who were able to get lunch there and that were just passing by there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It becomes totally unclear. Mr. Josse asked you about housing the leadership. You are now talking with a lot of details on when the hotel was built, which might not be that relevant, and you are now talking about giving lunches to persons. But are you talking about leadership personalities or are you talking about ordinary citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes ordinary citizens too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But most of what you described was a matter of accommodating the leadership? It sounds as if that was the bulk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was mostly the leaders, but it wasn't solely the leadership. From time to time, there were people who were very hungry and asked whether they could eat something there, and we would tell them that they could eat and then they would continue with their journey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but your main effort was housing and accommodating the leadership. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the hotel Panorama? How did that come to be used?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply, it was empty. There were no guests in that hotel. So that was the opportunity to put there people who had nowhere else to stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again here the question, what kind of people? What are we talking about? Are we talking about accommodating the leadership or are we talking about accommodating citizens, irrespective of their positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly the leadership. 90 per cent were the leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please be clear in your answers what we are talking about, because this is now the second time that it's unclear to me, when you're talking about persons, whether you mean those who are officials, leadership persons, or whether these are ordinary citizens. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I think I'll do is I'll come back to some of these issues a little bit later when we deal with them in another way. I'd like to turn now to Mr. Krajisnik, whom we've not mentioned -- or you've not mentioned at all in your evidence hitherto. When did you first -- and I'm not now talking necessarily about Pale in 1992; I'm talking about generally. When did you first become aware of the existence of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He appeared as the Speaker of the Assembly on television. He was the Speaker of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Had you met him prior to his being elected Speaker of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never even knew him. He did not take part in the activities of the party, inasmuch as I described that work here, in the flat of Mr. Karadzic. So he did not take part in the activities of the political party. He was not one of the founders, and he did not work in the advisory council. What surprised me, that somebody who was unknown would take upon him such an important position once the various upper -- topmost positions were divided between the Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In terms of his handling of the Assembly, you saw it on the television; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'm talking about the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly here, not the Republika Srpska Assembly. Did you ever go and watch him perform his tasks as Speaker of that particular institution?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether I attended the sessions of the Assembly or whether I saw them on television. I mostly saw them on television. I could read about it in the newspapers and we discussed it in the political council. Once or twice, by chance, I went to the Assembly as an observer, to see what it looked like live.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as -- and I know -- I'm deliberately going back in time. So far as the negotiations that took place in late 1991/early 1992, to try and avert a war was concerned, to what extent would you say there was any friction between SDS general membership and the leadership, and flowing from that, was that reflected at all in the political council?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not define it, but from the viewpoint of the political council, very often discussions were men saying that the leadership was too lenient, the leadership of the Serb Democratic Party. They complained that they were too indulgent towards the Muslims. Because with the Croats, the relations were much clearer. According to the assessment of the leadership of the SDS, it was very important to calm down the Muslims, to support them in the pre-election programme, in the sense that they should continue living in Yugoslavia and that they could stay on in Yugoslavia. And I think that was the approach that existed up until February or March, up until the moment, that is, when Mr. Izetbegovic and the SDA started finding ways and means of leaving Yugoslavia. That is the way how we thought about the things at that time. Mr. Radovan Karadzic was really in favour of calming that situation down, and he was heavily criticised because of that. At those first elections, Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. -- that is, Mr. Fikret Abdic was indeed the person who got most votes, and Mr. Izetbegovic came in second. Then ways were found of putting Mr. Fikret Abdic as the president of the Presidency, and then he was replaced by Mr. Izetbegovic. The leadership of the SDS did accept that, and that encountered this approval within the membership in general, and also in the political council. Well, the explanation was that we should be indulgent and try to come to an accord with the representatives of the Muslims. And Mr. Izetbegovic was the leader of the SDA, which was the party with the largest membership among the Muslims, and so we wanted to find the best solution for the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Divcic, these tensions that you mentioned a moment ago, between the leadership and the membership, were they ever reflected in discussions within the political council?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We heard very varied opinions, and there were also opposition -- there was also opposition that was voiced to such a way of dealing with the situation. But it was just a part of the political council that said that. But the political council was an advisory body, so there was a minority of the members of the political council who were flatly opposed to the replacing of Fikret Abdic by Alija Izetbegovic in the ways in which it was done. They thought that in such a way, the wishes and desires expressed through the ballot by the Muslims were really let down, and democracy was avoided in such a way, because most of the Muslims voted for Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, what about Mr. Krajisnik? How did he fit in, bearing in mind his role of Speaker of the Assembly, to these tensions between what I will call the SDS rank and file and the leadership?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. Mr. Krajisnik would only come when he would be invited to the meetings of the political council. I do not know what was his opinion about it. At that time, he was not in the leadership of the Serb Democratic Party, so I would not see them in those times. On television, I did not notice that he gave his opinion openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about the way he was handling the Assembly during this crisis? How was that viewed by SDS activists?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all surprised to see a relatively unknown person -- I believe that he was either sixth or seventh down on the list during the elections. So we were all surprised to see him occupy such an important position that was given to the representatives of the Serbian people, and we watched his every move very closely. Our estimate, the estimate of everybody, the Muslims and the Croats alike, was that before the open conflict started, that we managed to receive a compromise in the way the Assembly was chaired. And we all expected that the Serbian representatives would be given more opportunity to explain their political views. And this would have been a better solution. However, he didn't do this. Our impression was that he did everything but that, that he gave a lot more opportunity to the Muslims to say what they thought. And this caused some reactions in the political council, and I believe that he was invited to come and explain his position before the political council. He did that. He said that everything should be done to reach democracy, that we had just come out of a mono-party system, where nobody was allowed to say what they really thought, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, we're talking about a crisis, and it's not entirely clear whether we're talking about Assembly at this time, Assembly Speaker Bosnia and Herzegovina or the newly established or to be established entity of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Divcic, you heard the observation from the learned Judge. It's one that clearly needs to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the Assembly at the beginning of 1991, which was still a joint assembly, not a Serbian assembly. But the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the participation of everybody, the Serbs, the Croats, the Muslims and others who had organised themselves into political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about perceptions of activists and those on the political council - there are really two different questions here - as to Mr. Krajisnik's stance so far as the prevention of war was concerned?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of everybody - the Serb members and the Serb non-members, the ones that I worked with in the office - was that everything should be done to avoid war. During that period, during that stage, my impression was that amongst the common people that I spoke to, the Muslims and the Croats alike, nobody wanted to wage a war. They all supported a peaceful and sensible solution. I repeat: This was at the beginning of 1991, when Mr. Izetbegovic was still pursuing his pre-electoral political platform that won him so many Muslim votes. And this was staying in Yugoslavia. And we all knew that if we stayed in Yugoslavia, there would be no war, and we all knew that if a nation left Yugoslavia would mean a crisis that could grow into a war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, one question. We're talking about the political council and we are at the same time talking about the situation in the beginning of 1991. When exactly was this council established? Was that September 1991 or was it September 1990? I'm just ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] September 1990, before the multi-party election.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's my mistake. I should have looked it up in the -- yesterday's transcript. I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to jump forward a little bit, past the point where it became clear that the SDA leadership were advocating secession for Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia and to - I take this as an example - the Cutileiro plan. Bearing in mind what that plan would have meant to Bosnian Serbs, again, how was that viewed by SDS activists?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can only talk about the political council. At that time, I was not involved in the work of the SDS activists, as you call them. This was for us the last straw to cling on for Bosnia and Herzegovina not to enter a war. That's how we perceived this. Because of the developments in the past, the Cutileiro's plan was passed in March 1992, and the entire 1991 was marked by confusion, primarily due to Mr. Izetbegovic's positions, which changed overnight. And this all could be felt in the Assembly. We would leave our work places to watch the work of the Assembly to see what would happen, because this, to a large extent, determined how the crisis would develop, through the legal institutions. As for the Cutileiro's plan, in one part, and I would like to say that I don't know the details of that plan; I never held it in my hands; I have never read it or studied it, for that matter. But in one part, it guaranteed - at least, that's what they told us, our representatives tried to convince us of that - that this was the solution to avoid war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that this could satisfy the protection of the vital interests of all the three nations. Nobody would be able to achieve their maximum goals. Everybody would have to sacrifice something to keep the peace. We all had to reach a compromise. And that's -- I dare say, that that's how the majority of Muslims and Serbs perceived that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And again, dealing with the specifics, was there any reference within the political council to Mr. Krajisnik's part in the plan and his handling of the Assembly that was then in existence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout 1991, in January 1991 was still the time when the positions of Mr. Izetbegovic were very clear and were based on his pre-election programme. And then, overnight, the situation changed dramatically. I believe that Mr. Radovan Karadzic, at the meeting of the council towards the end of January, informed us that there had been a meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because my question -- perhaps I should have said. I was referring to the Cutileiro plan. In it I said "in the plan." So I'll read it again, the question. Dealing with the specifics, were there any references within the political council to Mr. Krajisnik's part in the Cutileiro plan and its negotiations and his handling of the Assembly that was then in existence in relation to the Cutileiro plan, please?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a question.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's actually two questions. The first one is the question about the political council. We did have a meeting sometime in mid-March. It was the extended composition of the political council. That's how we functioned. There were other members who were allowed to be there and say what they thought. We made very few decisions, so their voting right did not really matter. But when it comes to the Cutileiro plan and the proposal, whether the Serbian democratic party should be adopted or not, I remember that Mr. Radovan Karadzic was present at that meeting, Mr. Krajisnik was there as well, and they both supported the Cutileiro plan very heartily. They did have some reservations about it. I remember some of the interventions from the people who were not members of the council but were politically active, who very strongly rejected the plan, and they even threatened that the Serbian people would start a war if the plan was adopted. I remember that Mr. Krajisnik reacted on that occasion and that he said something to this effect: "Why do you say this? This has not been adopted yet. We have to discuss things and find our interest in all of this." I remember that discussion very well. I believe that this was the last or the penultimate meeting of the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I now want to turn, if I may, to Mr. Krajisnik's arrival in Pale. Do you recall when he arrived there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was among the last to arrive in mid-April. I'm not sure of the exact date. It may have been the 15th, the 16th, or the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What happened, if you have any knowledge of it, as to the physical housing of him and his family?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly where they were accommodated, because I was the one who provided them with the housing. They were lost, like everybody else. They didn't know what would happen to them. And I made sure that the family was accommodated in the Panorama. Mr. Krajisnik had a wife at the time and three relatively young children, of age [as interpreted], in any case. And I accommodated them in the Panorama, all of them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Divcic, you've just said "because I was the one that provided them with the housing." This is what I was trying to ask you about earlier, none too successfully on my part. What role had you undertaken to be the one who was providing people like Mr. Krajisnik with housing? Describe, in some detail, as far as I'm concerned, the job that you had taken upon yourself to do in this regard.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a weekend cottage for a number of years in Pale. I knew quite a lot of people, and I used my personal influence to do that. I'm not even sure that any of them -- or at least a majority of them would be able to find accommodation if I had not used my private, personal influence and friendship with the local population, who helped me in providing these people with accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how did you physically organise it? How did you go about it? Did you have an office? How did you decide who was going to go where? Those sort of details are perhaps important.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We improvised things. It was by and large improvisation. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. As for our office, there was a little Dobrotvor office there before the war, but it did not function properly. The Dobrotvor was at the beginning of its work. It didn't have any money. There were no people who worked for the organisation seriously. So it was very much an improvisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And now let's take Mr. Krajisnik as an example. He arrives in town. What happened? If you can remember. Did you get forewarning that he was coming? Did he arrive and come to an office? Did his wife come to an office? And how did you then decide - the second question - where exactly you were going to place him and his family?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. His wife did not come to our office, because I spent very little time in my office at the time. Truth be told, some other people told me that Krajisnik had arrived. I asked them if he had managed to find accommodation, and they told me, "We simply don't know what to do with him." Then I said, "Okay. I'll take care of him and his family." And that's when I found them this accommodation in the Panorama Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what sort of space did Mr. Krajisnik and his family have at the Panorama Hotel?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Panorama is a hotel which is far from luxurious. It was even in a very bad state of repair at the time, unfortunately. But that's what the conditions were at the time. I did not have any possibility to do anything else. We're talking about very simple rooms. Many of them did not even have a proper bathroom. People had to use a bathroom on the floor for all the rooms. It was a very simple accommodation. The rooms were humid, in a very bad state of repair. But that's what we had at our disposal at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you remember how much space Mr. Krajisnik and his family had?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they were given one or two rooms, adjoining rooms probably, with three or four beds. Four, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, the work that you were doing, the logistical work, were you being paid by anyone for it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some specific questions now, and we'll go back to what you were telling us about earlier. A consignment of aid, you've told us, arrived in Pale, is it, from various charities?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This consignment arrived from just one humanitarian organisation that was from Germany, and it had been organised by Mr. Steiner, whom I have already mentioned. He arrived from Zagreb, and I believe that this was in February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And where was this aid destined for?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was destined for the Merhamet, which was a Muslim humanitarian organisation, the Red Cross, and the Dobrotvor. And our allotment was some 30 per cent of that consignment. We basically cooperated, the three humanitarian organisations, we cooperated and we split this consignment rather fairly, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And where did the Dobrotvor part go to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have a central warehouse. One part went to Vojkovici, to the people that I personally knew, and I knew that there would be no abuse of that aid. Vojkovici also had a warehouse. Vojkovici is a part of Sarajevo. And one part went to Pale, to a Serbian man whom I knew, who also had a rather large storage space. And that's where we stored that part of the consignment. I know this person to this very day. I'm still on good terms with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek one clarification. Earlier it was said that Caritas was one of the receiving organisations and now the Red Cross appears, which of course is a totally different kind of organisation. Was that a slip of the tongue or was the Red Cross one of the receiving organisations? Because earlier it was Caritas and La Benevolencija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I said Red Cross, then I misspoke. I'm sorry. The Serbian Dobrotvor, the Croatian Caritas, and the Muslim Merhamet were the three humanitarian organisations in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you've described where the aid was stored, the Dobrotvor part of it, at least. What exactly -- how was it distributed from storage?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How was it distributed? In what manner? Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the situation and on the conditions. In Pale, according to some subsequent estimates, some 15.000 people came from Sarajevo. So from a town with 12.000 inhabitants, Pale became a town with 30.000 inhabitants. The aid was distributed based on another improvisation, but accompanied by proper documents. Everybody who needed aid were given aid by some volunteers, by people who volunteered to distribute this aid. At that time, I did not fear any abuse. I did not fear that this aid would be smuggled and sold on the black market. This was my main concern. At the beginning, however, at the time showed that my fears were not justified, that the distribution was fair and that the aid was -- reached the hands that needed it most. I remember that it was made public that the aid would be distributed on the main square, on a certain day, at a certain time, and that if people were there at the time with their IDs, they could be given packages so that they would have food over the next few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the shipment must be of some relevance. Looking at the time you spent on it. I don't know whether details as whether it was distributed on the market or on the streets -- could you please come to your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I'm going to move on. I really was hoping this was going to lead to another aid shipment which does have more relevance. Can I do that immediately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. And also please, in your questioning and in the way you proceed, don't leave it a big puzzle for the Chamber what the relevance of it is that you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm trying too hard not to lead, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that's bothering you. I'm looking at the Prosecution. I take it that if you would lead a little bit more, that's what I suggested at the very beginning of the testimony as well, that either Mr. Tieger or Mr. Harmon will jump up. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask you about -- I am going to lead a little bit, then. I want to ask you about another load of aid that was destined for Sarajevo itself, actually after the war had started, that had come from Serbia. Do you know what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I think we can take this quite shortly. This in fact was also going to be distributed by the four charities you had previously mentioned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The aid arrived, presumably, in lorries by land from Serbia and came to Pale, or near enough Pale; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It arrived in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You had a -- when was this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You had a problem. There was a war going on in Sarajevo and you had to get this aid to Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A huge problem, a major problem, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I want you to describe, fairly briefly, how you managed to solve this particular dilemma.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about this convoy from Mr. Krajisnik himself. He sent his driver to pick me up. I believe that it was during the night. When I arrived, he told me, very briefly, what that was all about, and he told me that he was not in the position to organise anything. He asked me to handle this consignment and to find a way to do it properly, by hook or by crook.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I just want to stop there. "Properly" meant what? I mean, that's perhaps really the point.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meant that I was given instruction saying that the aid was destined for Sarajevo, that it had to be distributed evenly among the four organisations, the three that I have just mentioned, the Muslim, the Croat, and Serb, and La Benevolencija, that was a Jewish humanitarian organisation. Our conversation was very brief, two or three minutes at the most, and then I asked him to give me his driver to take me to the warehouse in the Famos company. They had a large warehouse, as a company that had existed from before the war. I unloaded the aid in their storage. I left one part for the Dobrotvor, one fourth of the aid, and three-fourths I left in the warehouse. On the following morning, I organised a convoy of trucks. I transported the aid to Lukavica, to the Energoinvest company. This was also a part that was held by the Serbs. Since I could not take any chances with the loads of the drivers, I found a way through our office in Sarajevo, through the technical personnel that was still there. I asked them to get in touch with the Merhamet, the Caritas, and La Benevolencija, to ask them to organise themselves so as to be able to come to Lukavica to talk to me. I intended to give them their consignments. They did arrive. They told me that they had been shot at on the way. Mr. Tihomir Carkic was one of the participants in the meeting. Mr. Radomir Neskovic was also present. But I believe that he was there to talk about the Crisis Staff or something. In any case, he was not involved in this particular part of the humanitarian work. There was also a representative of the Caritas. He was a priest, but I don't remember his name. And Merhamet was represented by a man whom I knew. He was a paediatrician, and I believe that his name was Kerim Fazlic. Together with the aid that was loaded onto their trucks, they returned to Sarajevo and they distributed the goods there. I kept the Dobrotvor part, one part in Lukavica, and the other part in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I next want to ask you about whether there were any occasions that you can remember that you had dealings with Mr. Krajisnik where he assisted -- where he requested your assistance to help members of other ethnic groups during the course of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, may I just interfere. Have you finished with this special shipment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, I do understand that you want to inform the Chamber that Mr. Krajisnik cooperated fairly to the distribution of that aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why should we hear that it went to Lukavica and whether it was a paediatrician who came for Caritas or someone else and that it was later distributed over there? I mean, the message stops already on the moment, I would say -- or there's still something to come, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I don't accept that, for this reason, for the simple reason that the Prosecution may not accept this, and the details are important. The witness's recollection of who he dealt with, where he dealt with them, why he dealt with them, puts the whole story together, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And gives it an air of credibility, which is so important. Because I don't suppose Mr. Harmon is going to get up and say that Mr. Krajisnik was such a nice man and he was very keen to help Muslims during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But if the witness would have told us it was a surgeon rather than a paediatrician who came from Caritas -- unless Mr. Harmon has serious doubts as to the reliability in this respect of this witness. But it's a level of detail which, of course I do understand that you want to establish that this is a reliable witness, but I really wonder whether we're not going too far in a lot of details which -- let me just give the example of the paediatrician and the surgeon, which really -- I would not expect, as a matter of fact, Mr. Harmon to respond to that unless he would have serious reasons to believe that this whole story was not true. Please keep this in mind if you continue. I'm not the one who conducts the examination; it's you. And I do know what the practice is in your jurisdiction. But sometimes I really wonder whether it is of great assistance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Divcic, let's move on to another example, if you would, please. The question was whether you're able to give other examples of requests that Mr. Krajisnik made to you for assistance to be given to members of other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, quite often helicopters, military helicopters, would arrive from Serbia, carrying humanitarian aid. I can't tell you how much in quantity aid would come, as much as a helicopter can contain. So they would arrive and they would leave -- go back empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. Try and follow as best we can the learned Judge's instructions. There was an incident involving a helicopter. Helicopter arrives. What does Mr. Krajisnik say? I mean, that's the nub of it, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik came across me by chance and he asked me whether I could try and help some people go to Belgrade. He even thought that those people were Muslims, friends of -- some friends of his, and they asked him for help. And there was a family there with some plastic bags and they looked pretty disoriented. So I tried to help them and I put them on that particular helicopter. It is true that those people were Muslims. I asked them what I could do for them. They told me that they would like to go to Belgrade because they had family there. So I said that I will see whether I could do something about it. I asked the pilots to take them. The pilots did it really quite unwillingly, because it was against the orders. And I put that family on the helicopter and they flew away to Belgrade. I do not know who those people were. They never contacted me again. Even then, I did not know their names. But in principle, Mr. Krajisnik asked me then -- he told me, "Please, help all those people who need help." He probably thought that he had so many things to do and that he was quite exhausted, so he asked me that, in general, I should help all those people who were in need of assistance, regardless of who they were, Muslims, Croats, or even Serbs. But I had to organise it in the least for the Serbs, because they could simply take a bus and go to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In Pale, in 1992, was there a mosque?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, in Pale, no, not no 1992. There was not one before 1992. There isn't one there today. There is no mosque in Pale. There is only one Serb Orthodox church in Pale. And there is also a Catholic church there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you about whether there came a time where there were columns of Croat civilians who passed through Pale when they were fleeing from the conflict that they were involved in at that time with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inasmuch as I can remember, it was already in 1993, it was not only civilians but the soldiers as well, when a conflict broke out between Muslims and Croats, a large group of maybe some 1.000 combatants, under arms, and quite a large number of refugees, women and children, carrying bags in their hands, they were encircled by the Muslims. And there was no chance for them to go out of that blockade. And then the Serbs got there and gave them food and drink. And I watched it on television, and I watched the completely incredulous faces of the Croat soldiers. Because we were at war with them, and they could not believe that the Serbs could help them. And so they went through the Serb lines to the territory, to the zone controlled by the HVO, that is, the Croat forces. For them, it was completely unbelievable at the time that something like that could happen. Later on, we continued to fight, but we did let them go through our territory. It was a period of time when everyone was fighting everyone else. First the Croats and the Muslims were together against the Serbs. Then the Muslims started fighting the Croats, and at the same time, we fought the ones and the others. And in the end, the Muslims fought other Muslims. The forces loyal to Alija Izetbegovic fought the forces loyal to Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I next want to return, if I may, please, to events in Pale in 1992. To what extent did you have first-hand knowledge - and listen to the question carefully, please - did you have first-hand knowledge of the fact that Mr. Krajisnik's wife was injured in an incident and then subsequently died in a hospital in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met precisely in those days, whilst taking care of their accommodation, the wife of Mr. Krajisnik. I did not know her, but from what I could get, it was a very warm, modest woman who was solely interested in taking care of her family. And at various occasions, I brought relief aid to them so that they should not have to stand in the queue to wait for it. And I had heard that she was ill. So I would take that aid to them in the Panorama Hotel, in their room. It must have been around the 19th or the 20th of August, which is an Orthodox holiday, when Pale was shelled, and those shells fell around the Panorama Hotel. Mrs. Krajisnik was outside of her room, and I think that she fell down, and I think that she was injured quite seriously, not from a shell. That is what I heard. But I arrived there straight away. She simply felt very ill suddenly, and it was an aggravation of the illness that she had at that time. So nobody knew whether it was a fragment from the shell that caused that or not at that time, and she was transferred to the medical centre and then she died.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, because I wanted to know whether you had first-hand knowledge of this. You didn't, is what you're telling us; is that right? People told you what had happened after the event? You didn't see Mrs. Krajisnik after she had been injured; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I heard all that a few hours after it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. We know she died. Mr. Krajisnik was left with three children. What domestic arrangements did he make for his children, please? That do you have some first-hand knowledge of; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber - you can be brief - what the domestic arrangements he made were for his three young children.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He continued to live in Panorama, where he used to live before, and his children were housed with the family they had in Pale. I believe it was his wife's family, one of his wife's sisters. And they went to school there. So I would meet them occasionally, because Pale is a small place and you are bound to come across people in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A lady called Ratka Savic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. But I always have problems in remembering -- in matching the names with the faces. I know that I do know her, but I can't remember straight away now. But what I certainly do remember is the house where they used to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Divcic, again, changing the subject somewhat: In 1992, in Pale, I want -- you had dealings with the four people I'm going to ask you about, Professor Koljevic, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and Mrs. Plavsic; that's right? You had dealings with all of them, to a greater or lesser extent; correct? You're nodding your head. You should say something, but the answer is clearly yes. Of those four people, which were you closest to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Mr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And was he someone you would actually, use the English words, obviously socialise with?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the age difference and a difference in education, I would not dare call myself his friend. But we would go for walks quite often together. He was a man who could be quite fun, and I liked his company. And according to what he would say to me, he liked my company. We would stop quite often, have a cup of coffee, and then we would discuss various things. He loved walks, and there are forests around, so he -- that's how we socialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about what he said -- had to say to you about Mr. Krajisnik. Did he say anything about Mr. Krajisnik to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, or else I can't remember that he told me anything of any importance and that it would be relevant for us today here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did he ever suggest that Mr. Krajisnik was a member of the Expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about Dr. Karadzic? You've described how you knew him well in 1989, 1990. This was only two or three years later. He was clearly very busy in 1992. Did you drink coffee with him, walk with him, at all?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On a few occasions, we did have lunch together, but that was by chance and there were other people present there. It was not the same kind of contact that I had with Mr. Koljevic. Maybe also because Mr. Karadzic was very busy. Maybe not. Maybe he simply didn't want it. But anyway, that's how things were. And our relationship was not a very close one, relatively speaking. I was able to go to his office without going through a special procedure if I needed for it, but I didn't do it, because there wasn't really a need for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Mrs. Plavsic, I have to say that our relationship was a warm one. We did not really discuss politics. She was in charge of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. humanitarian issues at that time. But even so, we wouldn't discuss it very often. I only know that we would greet one another very warmly when we would come across one another, and that was very often. Otherwise we didn't have very many things in common, which wasn't really necessary for that type of socialising that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sure I can lead on this. There come a time that she moved from the Panorama Hotel to Rajska Dolina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To Rajska Dolina, which is located at the summit of Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So, in other words, it's at a higher altitude than Pale?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 1.800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea why Mrs. Plavsic moved to the summit of Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never discussed it, and I would not dare guess what she wanted to do. The fact is, however, that Rajska Dolina was a quieter place than Pale, because Pale used to be shelled. I can't tell you that she was afraid and that then she decided to leave. But up there, the situation was much quieter and the comfort was much better. Because Panorama was really not a very comfortable place. So Rajska Dolina is some 12 or 13 kilometres away from Pale. It was at the top of the mountain and absolutely outside of the range of shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And finally, from this list, Mr. Krajisnik. What was your relationship with him in 1992, particularly in comparison to the other people I've just been through. You might want to use that as a gauge.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was the least close to him. Maybe that could be the answer to your question. We would not go together for a coffee, we would not walk around together, we would not socialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient moment? I want to speak to Mr. Krajisnik before I complete this examination. I want to say, he has been very helpful, as always. He provided me with a large amount of material. But I promised him I would spend some time with him in private before I completed my questioning, and I'd like to keep to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd like to have an early break for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would. I am very near the end, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if we have a break of half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are a number of matters I still want to deal with, Mr. Divcic. Firstly: As a member of the political council of the SDS, are you able to comment about whether there was a division in existence between the party institutions and the running of the government?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period of time are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, you tell us, if there is a difference. Let's first of all deal at the time that the political council was in existence, which is really up until the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a clear division in the functions. The party function, on the one hand, the political organ, the Assembly, chaired by Mr. Krajisnik, the group of Assembly members in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were clear distinctions in the functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about after the war had begun and the leadership moved to Pale? Only comment if you're able to.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then the functions were separated. The political council no longer had an occasion to meet. They still existed, but they didn't meet. All the other functions were separate. The government did one thing, the Assembly did another thing. The Presidency had its tasks. The Dobrotvor dealt with other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you about gentleman by the name of Dragan Djukanovic, please. When - and just answer this literally when - when did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it was before the 1990s, but just in passing, so we didn't really know each other. We only met properly when the party, the SDS, was founded, or after the first multi-party elections. That's when we met, and we started seeing each other on a regular basis. He was not a member of the SDS. He was the president of some other party. I believe that the name of that party was the party of federalists or something like that. I studied the programme of that party, and it was very similar, if not the same, as the programme of the SDS and the programme of the SDA, for that matter, and that was for all of us to stay in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I want to jump ahead to 1992 in Pale. Were you aware that Mr. Djukanovic had moved to Pale when the war had begun?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him up there. I would meet with him there, or bump into him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was his job? What was he doing in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw him, I asked him what he did there, and he told me that he was the advisor to President Koljevic. I checked that information with Professor Koljevic later on, and yes, Professor Koljevic confirmed that to me. And he explained to me that as many young people had to be involved in the work of the institutions, the like-minded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did he have any role or function with Mr. Krajisnik, as far as you were aware? This is Djukanovic I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Or at least I don't know of it. I believe that I would have learnt if that was the case. In that conversation, he told me that he was very happy, that he was appointed advisor to the vice-president of the Presidency, Mr. Koljevic. He never mentioned either Mr. Krajisnik or any other person, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I next want to ask you one or two matters to do with the Kikinda building. You gave some evidence, I think it may have been yesterday, about how that building came into existence, got its name. Again shortly, because I suspect most people here know this anyway, what function did the building perform in 1992 in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was actually the seat of the Assembly, the Presidency, the government, of all of the important things that were happening in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in that region, was happening in that building there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about its fabric, its condition, in 1992. What were the offices like? What was the furniture like, that type of thing, please?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not offices. This place was a motel, and we used kitchen tables instead of desks. There were one or two telephone lines which were not working properly. So again, we're talking about another improvisation. The conditions were not in place for any kind of serious work. Nevertheless, this was the most appropriate thing that could be had at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: By "appropriate," you mean the best -- there was no better option available?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you mentioned the telephone lines. I think you said there were one or two. Literally, one or two lines, so only one or two people could be on the telephone at any one given time. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If those two people were lucky enough to get through after having spent several minutes dialling a number. In that part of the Sarajevo Romanija region, some 30 kilometres of its size in various directions, one could not establish any sort of communication. I'm talking about this region because you could easily drive across that region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the last answer is not perfectly clear to me. "One could not establish any sort of communication." Is that to say, Mr. Divcic, that there was no possibility of telephone communication? Because at the same time you say that there were a few lines and it was difficult and that you had to dial several times. Is it to say that it was difficult or that it was impossible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There was a massacre of Serbs in a place called Zepa. You no doubt have heard about that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that incident at all. What I want to know is: As a result of that, was there an incident outside the Kikinda building?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you tell the Chamber about that, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were outraged. They had heard about the murders in Zepa, and they blamed the leadership and a bad organisation. I live very near Kikinda. On the following day, when I arrived there, I heard that some soldiers had --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Divcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're trying to find the context in time of this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Zepa incident took place on the 4th of June, if I'm not mistaken. This was the first time that the soldiers from Pale had met with the coffins that arrived in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not mention the year. Is that the 4th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I stopped you, Mr. Divcic. You said that you live very near the Kikinda. On the following day, when you arrived there, you heard that some soldiers had ... Take it from there, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some soldiers were being taken to some positions or were being brought to some positions. They were outraged by the murders that they had heard of and they opened fire on the Kikinda building in Pale as they were being brought to their positions. On the following day, when I arrived there, I was told that that had happened, and at the beginning, those who were in Kikinda thought that they had come under a Muslim attack. It was dark. It was during the night. And they were afraid that the Muslim forces had broken a line and that they had opened fire on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how was it ascertained that it was Serb forces that had done this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was never ascertained that it was the Muslims who did that. If that had been the case, they would have been prosecuted or somebody would have gone after them. And it was clear, on the following day -- I'm not aware of anybody being taken to task for having done that. But in any case, it is certain that it was not the Muslim forces who had done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one question to clarify. You said if it would have been the Muslims, they would have been prosecuted. That suggests - I'm just putting that to you - that if one would suspect that it was Serbs, that they would not be prosecuted; is that a correct understanding of your testimony or is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about war conflicts. They would not have been prosecuted and criminally charged. We would -- actually, the army would have been after them to physically destroy them. That's what would have happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the emphasis is that they would have gone after them rather than that they would be prosecuted. Yes. That's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I in fact next want to ask you about Muslim departure from Pale. The vast majority of Muslims who lived in Pale before the war left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you play any part in their departure?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware that they left?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who was responsible for organising their departure?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the municipal bodies on the initiative of the Muslims. There were some 3.500 of them before the war, and due to the situation and as a result of the death in -- deaths in Zepa and the murders of some youngsters on the 8th of June in Trebevic, and as a result of all the stories from the Serbian refugees about the killings of the Serbs who had remained in Sarajevo, who had not been able to leave Sarajevo because of the inner ring that had been established by the Muslim forces, and under their control, so nobody could leave the town, for all those reasons, the Muslims started to feel insecure and they asked for a meeting, as far as I know, with the municipal leadership. And they, in turn, asked for a meeting with the leadership, i.e., the Presidency. I know that from my conversations with Mr. Nikola Koljevic, in a chance meeting, he told me, "I'm sorry. I'm in a rush. We can't talk. The Muslims want to move out. They don't feel safe. I am on my way there to try and convince them, but they are safe, and try to convince them, if at all possible, not to leave, not to go anywhere from here." That was one of our chance meetings. On the following day, I believe it was, he told me -- we talked. I don't know whether I was successful. I'll talk to them again. After that, I didn't see him again, but I know that a whole convoy of buses was organised to transport the Muslims and their personal belongings. And they left Pale to go to Sarajevo, to the part that they wanted to go to, the part that was under the control of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about Professor Koljevic's role in their departure. You didn't attend any of these meetings. He told you about them in the way that you've just described; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've asked two questions. It's my fault.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. I did not attend any of those meetings. It was Mr. Koljevic who told me about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What would you say to the suggestion that Muslims were forced involuntarily to leave Pale?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that this is not true. However, I fully appreciate the uncertainty that they felt after the deaths of so many people in Pale. If I had been in their shoes, maybe -- actually, not maybe. I'm more than certain that I would have acted in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I asked you before the break whether Professor Koljevic had ever suggested to you that Mr. Krajisnik was a member of any Expanded Presidency, and you said no. I should perhaps have asked you the same question about Mrs. Plavsic and Dr. Karadzic. Did either of them ever suggest that Mr. Krajisnik was a member of an Expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about Mr. Krajisnik, in conclusion, your impressions of him, through really 1991, 1992. Did you get the impression that he was a popular figure amongst Serbs, first in Bosnia-Herzegovina and then in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "popular" in the Serbian language is mostly associated with some other profession. For example, a singer, a pop star, can be popular. But let me try and answer your question. The answer is no. On the contrary, that was not my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So what was your impression?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was held in high esteem. People believed that he would not betray them. After one or two years of the existence of the Assembly, we wanted to have firm people as members of our negotiating team, people who would not falter, who would not be bribed, who would not betray the Serbian national interest. And I perceived this as being the case, and I thought, and other people I spoke to, believed that Krajisnik would not be bribed and that he would not agree to something that would go against the Serbian national interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about his actual power? Are you able to comment upon that? Did you regard him, both from what you saw of him and from what you gleaned from other sources, as a powerful man?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only me. I personally did not consider him powerful, because I knew he was not powerful. Others also did not consider him powerful. He had his authorities, and those authorities were very much connected with the work of the Assembly. That's where he was. He was the Speaker for the Assembly, and that's where his authorities stemmed from. And save for that, he did not have any other authorities, nor was he powerful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you say: "I knew he was not powerful," what do you mean by the word "powerful"?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he had been powerful, he would have found accommodation for himself. He would not have asked me to do it. Maybe he would have helped me to find better accommodation than was my house at the time, where there was no electricity for a year while I was staying there. If he had been powerful, he would have been able to deal with his own problems on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that deals with personal power. What about executive power within the Republika Srpska? Are you able to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not have any executive power. He was the Speaker of the parliament. The parliament has its president and its members of parliament who decide. He had just one vote in the Assembly, not more than that. The way the parliament functions is for certain parties to have their groups of assemblymen. He did not even attend the meetings of the group of the SDS members when they had meetings during the breaks in order to agree on their position on a certain issue. The group of the SDS assemblymen in 1991 was presided over by Professor Vojislav Maksimovic, as far as I know. Not even there did Mr. Krajisnik have anything else but one simple vote. By definition, an assembly is a legislative rather than an executive body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for one clarification. You said, Mr. Divcic, "He did not even attend the meetings of the group of the SDS members when they had meetings during the breaks." Then you said: "The group was presided over by Professor Vojislav Maksimovic, as far as I know. Not even there did Mr. Krajisnik have anything else but one simple vote." On the one hand, you say he did not attend; on the other hand, you say he was not presiding, he had only one vote in that type of meeting. What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was misinterpreted. I was not talking about his attendance but about him being the leader of that group. It was his obligation to attend the meetings, but he was not the president of the group of SDS assemblymen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. That ends my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Harmon or Mr. Tieger, are you ready to -- it will be Mr. Harmon, I understand. Are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Divcic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Harmon, who is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Divcic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On your last part of your evidence, Mr. Divcic, did you ever attend any sessions of the Bosnian Serb Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me go to a portion of your evidence that was -- just before the break, you testified that you had -- were in Pale and you were completely surprised, in fact it was unbelievable that the Bosnian Serbs would let a thousand combatants from the HVO through the Serb lines. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you aware -- I'm sorry. Also, that this, as far as you can recall, took place in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it happened in 1993. I'm not completely sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in 1993, in Central Bosnia, a war had erupted between the Muslims and the Croats; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why I thought of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were cooperative arrangements between the Bosnian Serb army and the HVO in respect of that particular war, that they had become, in part, allies in that war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were agreements between the HVO and the VRS to permit civilians and combatants to go through the Serb front lines?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Divcic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Judge Hanoteau has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. I'd like to go back to the second instance in which you lost your job when you left Sarajevo to go to Pale. Yesterday, as I understood it, you lost your job because you held a political position. Could you tell us how you were fired, how you lost your job.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I simply stopped going to work because I stayed in Pale. The roads were cut. I was unable to go back to my apartment, let alone to go to work. And where I used to live was still no man's land, and one could go there. But had I gone there, my life would have been in danger Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and I saw no reason to go back to my flat. And as for going back to work, I didn't want to do that because the building was on the other side of the Miljacka, which was a dividing line between -- in the city. And everybody knew that I was politically active. Later on, in 1993, when a colleague of mine who used to work in the same office managed to get out of Sarajevo, he was a Croat and I helped him go to Belgrade, and later on he went abroad. What he told me then was, "You took the right decision because you would have been in trouble. Had you gone back to work, you would have been killed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you were not fired. You didn't go back to work, and as a result, you lost your job, and you said you did well to do so. But you were not expelled from work by anyone. In other words, you never received a decision whereby you had lost your job for a particular reason?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. It was only after the war just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Fine. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the -- yes. Just to confirm that I did work there for a number of years. I got from the company, that is, really the pension fund, a document stating that I work for the electrical grid up until the 11th of April, 1992, and that my job ceased -- came to an end on that particular date. No reasons were given in that document. But the reasons are very clear. I came across many Serbs who got out of Sarajevo and who were in a very similar situation that I was. Maybe they were much less known than I was, and they had really great difficulties in order to -- and they had difficulties to get out. Some of them simply disappeared, but those who went to work during that period of time, they were harassed whilst they were at work. And some of them were dismissed as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have another question to put to you, if I may. As far as the departure from Pale of Muslims is concerned, the question was put to you, and your counsel - I'm sorry - Mr. Josse asked you a number of questions regarding this particular issue. And you said: "I have perfectly understood the uncertainty which the Muslims must have -- uncertain positions the Muslims must have felt after so many people had died. Had I been in their shoes, I would have done the same." I'd like you to spell this out for us a little bit, because I was not in Pale at the time. What did you mean when you said this, when you said, "after the deaths of so many people"? What had happened in Pale? Why is it that the Muslims had rather leave? And could you describe these events for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the events, the first one happened on the 4th of June, in Zepa. The second one during a religious procession when the coffins arrived in the Serbian Orthodox church in the centre of Pale and when we were all gathered there to pay respects to the dead. And that was immediately before they were to be buried. So at that time, Muslim forces made an offensive out of Sarajevo and Trebevic, and the Serbs found themselves in great difficulties. Then the religious procession was interrupted. And over the microphone it was transmitted that all people who were capable to fight, go and put themselves at the disposal in Pale. So all young men that were able to fight left. Many heavy combats took place there, and many Serbs from Pale died in them. And then we have to understand that our neighbours, Serbs, are dying, and they were killed by some Muslims that were not from Pale. But they started feeling uneasy, because you can't control the father of a young man who died, who can -- carrying a gun, create havoc with his gun. So I understand them, as a man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, the Muslims left because they were afraid of reprisals?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the answers you have provided us with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Divcic, I have a few questions for you as well. First, in relation to the last questions put to you by Judge Hanoteau: This Zepa incident was in June, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in early June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there any movement of Muslims out of Pale before June?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, but certainly not in an organised way and not in any great numbers. The majority of Muslims remained in Pale. Everybody was expecting a political solution to the crisis. They didn't want to leave the place where they were born. These were local people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if I do understand you well, there was not a moving out of any significance of Muslims before June from Pale?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
