utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Are you aware, do you have any knowledge, of truck-loads of detained people coming to Pale, not as a final destination, either in May or in June, from elsewhere or from the Sarajevo area? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A convoy came. I believe some 600 men, able-bodied. So they came to Pale. I was not involved with that, and I didn't even see them. But from other people who saw that, I am aware of the fact. They spent a night in the sports hall in the very centre of Pale. They were to be escorted to Sarajevo under the control of the Muslim forces, and that is how it was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where did they come from? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently, some of them were volunteers. Those were the rumours at the time. And I can't tell you exactly whether some of these rumours were true, or which one was true. We heard that there were volunteers from Sandzak who wanted to help their Muslim brethren and then subsequently they were arrested. Another rumour was mentioning the environments of Bratunac or Zvornik. So various rumours were around, and I can't tell you which one was the true one. But certainly it was only able-bodied men who were in that convoy. There were neither women nor children, nor elderly people in that convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say there were neither women nor children. Is that what you were told? Because you --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that an event which caught some attention, 600 people arriving?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it did catch attention, because 600 able-bodied men on the enemy territory, you can expect them to become armed, and if there is any escalation, then there would be war, either that they would shoot upon you and you would shoot upon them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your conversations with people you met in Pale who had some authority - I'm not talking about ordinary citizens - was the matter discussed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never talked about that with the people who had authority in those matters. I only talked to ordinary people about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it the talk of the day, to say it in plain English, that this, well, substantive numbers --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you speak to anyone who had any personal knowledge of what happened, or was it just all rumours?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to somebody who had first-hand knowledge of it. He was in charge of the security of that group of people while they were in the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he tell you that these were only able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was amongst the others who told me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. The Panorama Hotel you were talking about, could you tell us whether it accommodated also citizens without any official position?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were there, housed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was their percentage on the whole of the population in the Panorama Hotel?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that most of them were in that category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I'm just trying to find out whether the Panorama Hotel was a place where mainly officials and persons of a -- were accommodated or whether it was --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a general place where everyone could be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. And out of the people that I knew, people who had certain positions, if I really try and think hard, I think it was only Mr. Krajisnik who stayed on the longest, up until the end, I would say, even after the war. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I could call them celebrities, could you tell us what other celebrities stayed there, although shorter?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic lived in a house that was within the compound, but it was a separate house. However, it belonged to the Hotel Panorama. It was a house there. And he spent some time there with his family. I did not take part in organising his accommodation. At the start, there was an idea that in the Kikinda building, because it had rooms where people could sleep, some important members of the leadership should be accommodated there with their families. But later on, they abandoned the idea because they thought that family life would be a nuisance to the work of the institutions. Later on, there was Biljana Plavsic as well, but I did not take part in organising her accommodation either. And I believe Nikola Koljevic never lived there. I know that he was all the time in Pale. I can't tell you exactly where he lived. But there were also other people there in passing, some ministers who spent some time there waiting to find a better solution. Some people would spend a few nights there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. If you'd just give me one second. You told us that Mr. Krajisnik would only come to the meetings of the political council if he was invited. Could you tell us how often he was invited? I think you said that altogether there were some ten meetings. Is that correct or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some ten meetings? I do not know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that's a mistake. Please tell us how often you met and how often Mr. Krajisnik was invited.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political council met after the elections every week. I am sure that they met every Monday at 6.00 p.m., in the offices of the party. Mr. Krajisnik did not attend the meetings very often. He would only come when invited, when the members of the council wanted an explanation in relation to his work in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us a few examples of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, Mr. Izetbegovic is moving slightly away from his intention to have a united Bosnia and Herzegovina within Yugoslavia, and there was a animated debate in the Assembly about that. There was an attempt at that time to pass the so-called declaration on the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Assembly. That declaration was redacted in such a way that it implied that the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina is derived from the citizens themselves and not by taking into account the sovereignty of every constituent people. The Serb members of parliament thought that it would be a trap because you would then introduce the principle of one man, one vote, which -- it's not unusual in countries with only one nation who lives there and that are well organised. But this was not a one-nation country, and if there are 20 members of parliament, then they can make a proposal, in writing, to put to bill for reading at something that is called the Council for the National Equality, and that is the body which stopped the declaration. And that was the topic on the agenda of the council, because it was not to be permitted to introduce the one-man, one-vote system. The Serbs were proposing something called the chamber of the peoples, a body that would have a right of veto and that would provide the vital national interests of every people. If I may add, by the way, that the lawyers interpreted that as being anti-constitutional and that is something that was discussed at the council. Later on, the declaration was imposed by a majority vote. In the meantime, somewhere in mid-1991, Alija Izetbegovic made a speech. In his speech, he was less strict than in the declaration, but he implied that if Slovenia and Croatia would leave Yugoslavia, that Bosnia and Herzegovina could follow suit. And the Assembly procedure in those matters, if I remember well, was of a qualified simple majority. And there was a newspaper that was called, I think, Muslimanski Glas, that is, the Muslim voice, they published an article that saying for some unjustified reasons, five or six members of the parliament were not in the parliament on that day. And that is why his proposal was not adopted, because there's only one Muslim vote that was missing in order for that declaration to be adopted. There is something else that I remember that Mr. Izetbegovic said, and that really had great echo in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can I go on? Well, he was the president of the Presidency, which means that he was also the president of the largest political party, the largest Muslim party. He said, "We are going to sacrifice peace in order to have a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina." That was like a bombshell. That was a declaration of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were there -- first of all, I'd like to ask you, because my question was about the presence of Mr. Krajisnik in the political council. You explained as an example, although quite a wide range of matters. What did you need Mr. Krajisnik for to discuss this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wanted him to share with us his impressions. We wanted to be recipients of the first-hand information rather than those who would receive information from TV and newspapers. We were also duty-bound and we also had a moral obligation to listen to him, and it was also his moral obligation to come and talk to us about his first-hand knowledge. Very often during those breaks, things were being said that were not broadcast on television, and he was the one who was best suited to tell us what they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I have to understand this last part of your answer that, well, part of the political debate took place not in public, in parliament, but that the meetings of the members of the Assembly during the breaks were of importance for choosing positions and -- is that how I have to understand the last part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me give you an example that has nothing to do with Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Karadzic said, for example, at the council that the Muslims in the Assembly were aware that this initiative, this declaration, could be blocked in the way that I have just described. And in the break, he was told, "If you block this, if you prevent this from happening, we will advocate confederation, together with Slovenia and Croatia." Those were unofficial conversations, outside the Assembly. There was also another unofficial story that Mr. Karadzic shared with us, that only Muslims and Croats would secede and join Croatia. I'm still not sure until this very day how they planned to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it seems that you're mixing up now two things. I asked you about meetings of the members of the Assembly, and I understood these meetings to be meetings of members of one of the parties, whereas you just explained to us what the conversations were about on an inter-party basis. I asked you about whether these meetings where the members of the Assembly belonging to one party, and of course then I'm referring to the SDS at this moment, whether these meetings were of importance for, well, making up your mind, choosing positions, matters that were not openly discussed during the Assembly meetings.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes yes, sometimes no. Those were unofficial, informal conversations during the Assembly session breaks in the corridors, and it all depended who said what, with what particular political weight and who those things were said to. However, because of the overall atmosphere and of everything that was happening, we simply wanted to be privy to all the aspects of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you're talking about conversations in the corridors, but you earlier talked about a meeting of Assembly members belonging to a specific party not being presided over by Mr. Krajisnik. That sounds different from occasional meetings in corridors. That sounds like meetings, where you usually are in the same room, where you close the door when the meeting starts. Have you any personal knowledge of it? If not, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no personal knowledge, because I did not attend those meetings. Only assemblymen could attend those meetings. As the name has it, it was the group of the assemblymen of the SDS party. And this was their official position and this is what we could watch on TV. It was that position that they spoke about openly. They presented it publicly at the Assembly meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does this answer also imply that you do not know how these meetings actually were conducted? You told us that Mr. Krajisnik was not presiding over these meetings. What's the basis of that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the book of rules of the work of those groups. This is a common procedure. I know who the president was at the time. I believe that that was Professor Vojislav Maksimovic, and he should have done it by the book. I never saw him chairing any of these meetings. I was never in the room where those meetings were taking place. However, the logic of the whole thing implies that things should have been done by the book. There was a book of rules that governed those meetings. I hope I've been clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you have no information about how these meetings really took place?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, for those answers. Have the questions of the Bench raised any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got one question in fact that arises from Mr. Harmon's cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I've got one question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have asked you before, as a matter of fact, Mr. Josse. Apologies for taking the wrong order. But now you have it all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Exactly. I assume, bearing in mind how short the cross-examination was, that was what Your Honour was doing, and if I may say, with respect, it seemed a very sensible course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were asked whether you had attended any sessions of the Bosnian Serb Presidency and you said that you had not attended any such sessions. Did you attend any sessions of the Republika Srpska Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an observer, when they took place in Pale, I was there very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And are you able to say how many times you attended such sessions?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five, six, seven, eight. I attended those that I had an opportunity to attend if I had the time, when my duties permitted me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The other issue I want to ask you about is you were asked some questions about your knowledge of the group of people that were detained in the sports hall in Pale, and you said that though you had no personal, first-hand knowledge of it, you spoke to someone who did have first-hand knowledge, and in fact you specified in your evidence what their role was in the detention of these individuals. Just yes or no: Are you prepared to name that person?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Stevica. He resided in Pale. I can't remember his last name at the moment. He got killed towards the end of the war, actually. I know that he was an athlete. I knew him rather well. I can't remember his last name, but I can let you know what it is later on. His name was Stevan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Going back to the other topic I wanted to re-examine you on, namely, the issue of meetings of the Assembly, the RS Assembly. What period are we talking about that you attended meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended one or two sessions, maybe, in 1991, that is, before the war or the conflict. And the others I attended during the period between 1992 and 1995. And even after the war. After the first multi-party elections after the war. Those meetings often took place in the Bistrica Hotel on Mount Jahorina and I was there. Some of them I can still remember. I can tell you about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about that. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Divcic, Judge Orie asked you some questions about the 600 people who were able-bodied men and who were brought to Bratunac and detained in the sports hall. Can you tell us, please, the distance between the sports hall and the Kikinda building?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three to four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the distance between the Panorama Hotel and the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two, three.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what is -- was there a police station that was next to the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, actually, very close to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the distance between the police station and the sports hall, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are separated just by one street.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This, then, Mr. Divcic, concludes your evidence in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to answer questions of both parties and of the Bench, and I hope you'll have a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Divcic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I mention a brief procedural matter that flows, really, from what's just happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'd observe this as well, the same happened with the last witness, Mr. Vasic. I'm not saying there's a great deal of importance in what I'm saying, but I think it is worth mentioning and the Chamber clarifying the position here and now. In our submission, the correct order of questioning after questions from the Bench are Prosecution and then Defence. In effect, the party calling a witness should be entitled to ask the witness the last questions, as long as, of course, as the questions are asked, arise either from cross-examination of the Prosecution or cross-examination -- or the questions asked by the Bench. That, in our submission, is the proper procedure that should be adopted from now on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give it some thought, Mr. Josse. Now and then you tell us that coming from a certain jurisdiction, that you have some difficulties in finding your way through this system. You'll understand that I come from a system, and as a matter of fact, all three Judges come from a system where it's always the Judges who finally conduct the examination of witnesses, added and assisted by the parties. So I certainly take it -- I take your suggestion, think it over, and if I agree with you, and why would I not agree with you, then we'll certainly adopt that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I say, I accept that in the event that the Prosecution ask questions and the Defence then wanted to ask further questions that arose, I have little doubt that the Bench would allow the Defence to do that. Having said that, in my submission, it would be better to regularise things in the way that I've suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I fully agree with you that if it were only that everyone knows what to expect, that we should regularise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are a number of procedural issues outstanding. The Chamber, of course, is -- did not expect the cross-examination would take that little time, and therefore, we had in mind after this break to -- after the break to come, to deal with these procedural matters. I haven't got everything in front of me which I would need to deal with the procedural matters, so I suggest to the parties that we have a break of the normal length and then deal with procedural matters on from a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's satisfactory, Your Honour. One procedural matter we would like to deal with, outstanding, and just to put on the agenda, is the issue of Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was, as a matter of fact, one of the things I had in mind. We have some others as well, such as -- perhaps not something to be discussed at this moment, but from my memory, I say that on the 3rd of November, that the time-limit for, well, giving names of experts or at least informing the Chamber about expert reports expires, so the Chamber is very much interested to know whether sufficient progress has been made in order not to be surprised by the 3rd of November. These are matters I'd like to discuss after a break of 25 minutes. So we'll resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.text: I'd first like to deal with the exhibits that have been tendered in relation to the testimony of Witness Vasic. utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With respect, I agree. Perhaps the Prosecution would let me know formally in due course how it is they only have that extract from whatever was filmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE

And in my submission, it's not an unreasonable reaction and I endorse it on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm confident that this matter can be arranged out of Court, and if there's any need for the Chamber to further intervene we'll hear from the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER

utterances.text: Yes. Then other matters. I'll raise only a few. I think the Defence announced that it would be in a position to further comment on the Davidovic issue, if I may call it that way, once we had started the case. Mr. Stewart or Mr. Josse. I don't know who is dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, really, obviously internally, we deal with it in particular ways. But Your Honour, once again, I believe what the Defence announced was that it would only be in a position to further comment on the Davidovic issue sometime after we had started the case. I can comment on it to this degree, Your Honour: We are working on it. But there are very distinct limits to the time we have at our disposal to work on it, particularly as far as counsel is concerned. But with suitable delegation, we have been working on it, and I've discussed it again very recently with Mr. Josse, and some progress is being made. However, Your Honour, beyond that, if we are talking about a wholesale examination of this issue and an attempt to fully explore and discuss the concerns expressed by the Prosecution, then I'm afraid that must still lie some little way in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence is ordered to give its response by the 15th of November and not one day later, of course unless good cause shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does good cause include other demands on the Defence time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good cause is always valid in this courtroom, as you may know by now, Mr. Stewart. The next issue is whether the Defence could give us an indication on whether there would be any reason to doubt that there would not be the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 3rd of November limit as far as experts are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there's serious reason to doubt that, for a similar reason to the one I just expressed. Your Honour, we are simply unable to cope with assault demands on our time, including the ones I mentioned the other day, which were expressly brought to the attention of the Trial Chamber when we made our application for extension, some of which still remain unstarted, let alone unfinished. Your Honour, we -- it is most unlikely that we are going to be able to do that by that date, because there are matters which absolutely have to have priority. With the greatest respect, Your Honour, they just do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me say the following: We have been this week in Court time available 16 hours. We've heard two witnesses. I think they were scheduled both for four hours. We used less than 12 hours. And it seems that for next week we only have scheduled -- it's again a short week of only four days -- that we might end up in a similar situation. The Chamber wants to express quite clearly that this is not how we're going to proceed. The Chamber granted some time to the Defence to get their engine on the right temperature and on the right speed. But the Chamber did not have in mind that it would be finally the Defence, or the claim by the Defence, how much time they would need that would be determinative for this trial. The Chamber will spend quite some time tomorrow morning on considering the issue. A few items and our agenda are more close monitoring on how the preparation of the presentation of the Defence case, how it -- what progress is made in that respect. We also think about such measures as ordering the Defence to come up soon with a list of witnesses which gives the Chamber a better impression of what the Defence case will be, so that the Defence will have to make some choices. The Chamber is very concerned about the present situation, and the Chamber will not accept that all time-limits set, and in the argument we heard from the Defence, a lot of attention is paid to what we did not grant, lesser attention is paid to the flexibility the Chamber has shown and the additional time, although, as the Chamber understands, in the view of the Defence, insufficient, has been granted. Let me take the example of the experts. That is a -- I'm not saying it's a simple matter, but it's relatively simple and it's relatively -- it's consuming relatively little time. I'm not saying it doesn't take any time. The Chamber is not willing, as far as such a list of experts is concerned, to say not the 3rd of November, then perhaps the 30th of November, if we set a new time-limit, then the 15th of December, if not, the 15th of January. There comes a point where the Chamber may say, if there's no list by that date, then there are no experts. As I said before, the Chamber will take ample time tomorrow to further deal with the matter. The Defence should already prepare to see whether they can fill next week, either through witnesses that are nearby, in whatever way. But the Chamber will give the parties the result of its deliberations of tomorrow in the beginning of next week. We'll adjourn --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, would Your Honour please, with the greatest respect, would Your Honour please just hear the Defence on one or two aspects?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, Mr. Stewart, the Chamber heard the Defence as far as extension of time is concerned at quite a number of occasions. But if there's anything new you'd like to add at this moment, you'll have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is this: I will say, Your Honour, that I personally, and I'm speaking personally now, have every reason to feel misled and up to a point cheated by this institution, and I will make that strong assertion good. When we first came into this case, I was told that it was expected that the trial would -- could be ready to begin at the beginning of December 2003. It is impossible to understand how that could responsibly and conscientiously have been said to me, and I made my assessments of this case based on what I was told then. It is impossible that it could have been ready by that time. I was also told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I interrupt you. This sounds not really new to me, because you have expressed at earlier occasions that, on the basis of what you heard at that time, that you got an impression which turned out to be wrong and that you're blaming those who gave you the information at that time for giving that information. That's not new to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll leave that one, then. What is perhaps new is that I was also expressly, because I made express inquiries, I was expressly led to believe that the schedule for the trial would provide at least some regular gap during the progress, because I made it perfectly clear that, as a practicing barrister, I did need to have some such gap. I was assured that would be so. It hasn't happened, which causes tremendous difficulty. Your Honours, bringing the matter right up to date, on that list that I gave to Your Honours, and I'm asking, it's embarrassing to have to do this, but I am asking to have this taken into account, on that list I draw express attention to the fact that I have the responsibility as lead counsel to file an end-of-stage report. I have 120 days from the end of the stage to do that, and I'm up to about 90-something days now since July the 22nd. That is a very time-consuming task. It took a great deal of time in relation to the previous stage, and it has taken and will continue to take considerable time in relation to this stage. Your Honour, my team are all paid up front. I am not. I do wonder whether there is anybody else in this courtroom who has had to accept several months' delay in their pay in relation to this matter. That is part of my management responsibilities to my team and to myself. I have to find time to do it. And I put it forward for this reason, Your Honour, that why would, and I ask rhetorically, why would Your Honours suppose that I would have continually deferred that task unless I had had to? It is absolutely obvious that I could and would only have deferred that task for so long if I had had other, as I have had, other pressing priorities which have constantly prevented me from being able to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, Mr. Stewart, Mr. Stewart, I'm going to interrupt you. The matter is new to the extent that it relates to the last couple of months. The matter is not new because it is an aspect of the problem which you have brought to our attention several times. So we do understand that this has not changed for the last couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But Your Honours never respond to it. And you haven't responded to what I said the other day, and you didn't respond to what I said before. I constantly raise these matters and Your Honours constantly ignore them and brush them aside, as if they're not part of the real world. You do not show sufficient interest and concern about the position of the Defence. You do not inquiry properly as to what the matters which are actually affecting the Defence, and that has been the position throughout this trial. And the result is that Your Honours constantly impose oppressive and unconscionable burdens with shocking results that we saw during the progress of the last few months of the Prosecution case and with a build-up of undone tasks that this Defence team cannot possibly cope with. And there's a longer list. We are struggling. We have thousands and thousands of pages of transcript. We don't have time to read it. We don't have time to go back. We don't have time to do these things. The dossiers that came one after another in July, it was impossible. Ms. Loukas had no time to look at those. I had no time to look at those. Nobody has time to look at those on the Defence side. And the position gets worse and worse and worse. And Your Honours wonder why we don't do these things, and the answer is because we can't do them. Because you ask us to do too many things too quickly. It's getting worse and worse and worse. It just piles up and piles up and piles up and we cannot cope. And in the awkward and embarrassing areas that I've mentioned this morning, we are also entitled to deal with those. I have to deal with those matters. They are part of my job as lead counsel. They're part of my responsibility all round. You have to give us, with the utmost respect, Your Honour, you have to revert to something nearer or better than we have now. There was a time when the progress of the Defence case was supposed to include one week off every five weeks. That's got lost in the wash. We're relentlessly being pushed along. The last few months of the Prosecution case were an appalling burden on this Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, this sounds very much as a repetition of what we heard before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps Your Honours will listen this time for once so I don't have to keep repeating it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the idea of repeating it, and you are blaming the Chamber for not paying attention to it and not responding to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That is my submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's your submission. I'll say a few words about that before we adjourn. The Chamber, of course, has spent a lot of time on deliberations on what is fair and what would not be fair to the Defence. The Chamber has deliberately decided, as you may have seen in our earlier decisions, that we work on the basis of an assessment of what is needed to prepare this Defence. We will not, and if that's your expectation, then perhaps you could consider to leave it behind you, we will not review the way the Defence team spends time on administrative matters, experts, et cetera. I think you would not even want us to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do in fact wish you to listen. We do not wish the Trial Chamber to be troubled with trespassing on unnecessary and troublesome detail, but yes, we do wish the Trial Chamber clearly to understand demands on our time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I prefer if you would not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Listening is something different from giving our judgement on that it is fair to spend now three and a half days on administrative matters because it would be unfair for person X not to receive money and person Y could wait for a couple of days, and that is to be -- should be a priority to experts or whether experts would be a priority to the preparation of proofing of witnesses. We are carefully listening, and as I said before, you spend a lot of attention to where we did not grant it, we did not grant what you asked for. It's not the case that we never grant or that we do not partially grant what you ask for. But finally, the fact that the Chamber does not allow the Defence the time it asks for, even that the Chamber, as I understand, in the Defence's view, does not allow the Defence the time, it doesn't ask for, but would be absolutely minimal to even present a shade of a defence - that's how we understand the position of the Defence - does not mean that we are not listening. The Chamber has its own responsibility in judging, in determining what is needed for the preparation of the defence. We'll further consider the matter, as I said, tomorrow morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I inquire something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, just questioning what is precisely the purpose and the point of the meeting that Your Honours referred to tomorrow. I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If Your Honours are not wishing to receive any information from the Defence as to the demands upon our time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that I gave you an opportunity to add whatever you wanted to add to what has been said before. I noticed that most of what you said was not new, or only relatively new to us. We'll meet tomorrow and we'll see what --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The Judges are going to meet or are all of us to meet, Your Honour? That's what I'm not clear about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About the meeting of tomorrow, it will be a meeting of the Judges. It was just to indicate that we'll come up with further rulings, guidance, whatever assistance of the Chamber on practical matters in the beginning of next week and that we will pay proper attention to it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, can I say, for example, I didn't come down today equipped to deal with this matter, not fully. Your Honours say that we've been having -- we have had an opportunity of adding. I came down for a completely different purpose. But, Your Honour, this Defence is working. I've actually been working since 5.15 this morning trying to sort out some of these very difficult financial issues in relation to resources, which are also included in my responsibilities. We are not just sitting around not doing anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart, the Chamber does not say that you're just sitting around. The Chamber says not whether you have to get up at 4.00 in the morning or 8.00 or 10.00. The Chamber finds on its experience in the case, on what has been done in the experience of the Judges of this Chamber, what it takes to prepare. We have to assess what is fair and we should give the Defence the time we consider to be fair. And the mere fact, and it comes -- it seems that it comes down to that more and more, the mere fact that you consider the time not sufficient and that the Chamber considers a certain amount of time sufficient, that fact, as such, could not automatically lead to following the suggestions of the Defence rather than meeting our responsibilities as a Chamber, responsibilities both towards this institution and the international community and, I would say, in the first place, our responsibilities in granting a fair trial to Mr. Krajisnik. If you say, "We can't do it within the time allotted by the Chamber," you might have to consider whether to adopt other procedures, to prioritise in a different way, exactly the field in which the Chamber is not going to tell the Defence what to do. The Chamber is not going to tell you that instead of getting up at 5.15 this morning, you should have got up at 4.15. That's not for the Chamber. The Defence, in the time assessed by the Chamber to be fair time for the preparation of the defence case, will have to do it within that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Maybe one day the Chamber will tell me I should have got up at 6.15. Your Honour, we wouldn't make such an absurd submission as to say that the mere fact that we consider there's not sufficient time, et cetera, et cetera, to lead to those results. What we do say is this, Your Honour: Your Honours have indicated, and of course you have experience and so on, Your Honours have indicated you will form an assessment. What the Defence is suggesting is that the assessment would be better reached if the Trial Chamber receives and waits for some facts from the Defence. And we expressed concern, for example, there was a good illustration of how a conclusion can be leapt to which is wrong, in the reference made in Your Honour's recent decision on self-representation to resources, which Your Honour's view of that term was in fact quite misconceived. And if you had consulted and had submissions on that, it would have been plain. But the trouble is that when Your Honours produce these matters without telling the Defence what the parameters are, what the concerns are, what assumptions you are making, without giving us a chance to answer it, there is a heavy risk it will lead to an unfair result. We are happy, Your Honour, simply to have the opportunity to explain to the Trial Chamber why we say we don't have enough time. In the end, it's -- of course, it's the Trial Chamber's decision. No assertion on the Defence part carries the day. It's up to the Trial Chamber. But facts are facts, and where they are available to either replace or improve or supplement Your Honour's assumptions and assessments, then, with the utmost respect, they should be sought and they should be considered. And there are facts, and not all the facts are before the Trial Chamber, and I didn't know I was going to have to deal with this issue today. I was in fact waiting, as Your Honour promised me. You said you would go away and consider the point which I raised earlier this week and I had given Your Honours, with respect, time to do exactly that and was awaiting Your Honour's response to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if there are any facts which are relatively simple to write down or to understand, the Chamber will include them in its deliberations tomorrow morning. If we do not receive anything , and this is because you are so specifically asking for it, if we do not receive anything, we'll -- part of our deliberations will also be whether we'll give you another opportunity to present any further information. But I think it would be more efficient that if there are -- of course, if you want to write down a whole analysis of the way the Defence used its time until now, then of course the time would not be sufficient. But if, by way of example, if you would say the Chamber certainly is not aware of the fact that the whole of the support staff suffered a three-week flu attack which has really changed the situation dramatically, of course we would like to be informed about these kind of matters and then a short message would do for the time being. We are at a time where we have to adjourn. We adjourn until next Monday, a quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
